name: The Five Magical Materials (Jade, Soulsteel, Moonsilver, Starmetal, Orichalcum)
summary: Summary of this book's lore/forging notes for each of the Five Magical Materials, including the Sidereal-specific and grim account of how starmetal is actually produced (an audited, condemned minor god's Essence, executed and cast down to Creation for a Sidereal savant to collect).
mechanics: Jade: the only Magical Material forgeable by ordinary Terrestrial techniques (carving with diamond-tipped tools, since it cannot be hammered unless heavily alloyed with steel); its five colors each correspond to one of the five elements and can only augment Aspect Abilities/Charms of that element. Soulsteel: alloyed from Labyrinth ore and the souls of the dead via Craft (Soulforging); mortals need a Valor roll (difficulty 2, or 1 for Dragon-Blooded) just to touch a soulsteel artifact and suffer a die penalty using it (other Exalted are immune), and any living being of Essence 3 or less other than a Solar must make a Valor roll (difficulty 1) when facing a soulsteel weapon; soulsteel weapons gain +1 Accuracy and soulsteel armor grants two extra soak dice. Moonsilver: purified from Wyld chaos by Luna herself, now found almost exclusively in the Wyld; forging requires harvesting ore under moonlight with no crafted tools (Intelligence + Lore roll, difficulty 3), purification rituals known to No Moons (or learned by other Lunars over 6-minus-Essence years), and working only at night with unpolluted fuel and moonlight-only water; non-Lunars who wish to use moonsilver artifacts must pass trials akin to the Silver Pact's rites of passage (see merit-moonsilver-initiate). Starmetal: the rarest Magical Material, popularly said to be refined from a fallen star, but actually the Essence of a minor god condemned to death by the Bureau of Destiny's audit process (see Exalted: The Sidereals, pp. 34-40) and cast down for a Sidereal savant to collect and forge; once collected it can be worked with ordinary mundane tools like any other metal, and is especially prized for the pens Sidereals use to write prayers to the pattern spiders. Orichalcum: mined from deposits (heavily guarded since the Usurpation) or refined from natural gold via a lava-heated solar forge and mirror-focused sunlight (Intelligence + Craft [Orichalcum] roll, difficulty 3); it alone of the Five Magical Materials can embody perfection and suits any artifact purpose, destructive or restorative.
compatibility: Reference material underlying the Artifact Background and artifact-creation rules for any Exalt; the starmetal entry is specifically relevant to Sidereal-sourced artifacts.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Ingredients of Wonder' -> 'Magical Materials' -> 'Jade'/'Soulsteel'/'Moonsilver'/'Starmetal'/'Orichalcum', printed pp. 37-40 (PDF 38-41).

name: Exotic Ingredients: First Age and Age of Sorrows Examples
summary: Two GM-facing sample lists of setting-flavored exotic ingredients an artificer might use to seed an artifact's Essence pattern: five First Age examples (mostly synthesized/conjured) and ten Age of Sorrows examples (mostly gruesome trophies and salvage), each with a brief mechanical hook.
mechanics: Five First Age examples: distorted Half-Damned blood (for devices delving beyond Creation or penetrating demons' defenses); elemental salt-diamonds (removes an artifact's otherwise-unavoidable Drawback); a mortal warrior's perfect-strike kata etched and traced onto weapons (+2 dice to wielders' Melee attack pools); a compressed dragon-track/Demesne rod (lets an artifact draw Essence directly from a Demesne without a Manse or Hearthstone); spiritual drilling rigs into the Labyrinth (all destroyed in the Contagion). Ten Age of Sorrows examples: ground dust of broken artifacts (-2 to a similar item's construction difficulty); vented failed/wild Hearthstones (-•• Essence Drawback); Fair Folk blood-flowers mixed with the artificer's blood (infuses a Virtue rated 4+ into the item for a related passive benefit); a god's eyes (potent Essence source, legally fraught to obtain); a thread from a Maiden's robe (aids artifacts under that Maiden's colleges); a Solar's own bones (necromantic feedback loop, draws Deathlord attention); dragon's blood (81 drops, potent but hazardous to harvest); distilled Heavenly Quintessence/Ambrosia; Wyld constrained in moonsilver chalices (forced into complementary shapes near an unfinished artifact); and lightning-fused desert obsidian (used by the artificers of Gem).
compatibility: Storyteller/artificer-player tool for flavoring new artifact designs for any Exalt, including Sidereals.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Exotic Ingredients' -> 'Five Sample Exotic Ingredients Used in the First Age' / 'Ten Exotic Ingredients Used in the Age of Sorrows', printed pp. 40-41 (PDF 41-42).

name: Collar of Dawn's Cleansing Light (Artifact •)
summary: Level One sample artifact: a piece of neck jewelry (collar, choker, torc, or delicate necklace) that keeps its wearer immaculately clean and bolsters her resistance to disease and poison, common enough that many Dragon-Blooded wear one simply to show off.
requirements: Attunement (1 mote of Essence).
mechanics: Negates all Social-roll penalties for being dirty or unkempt, regardless of actual conditions (the wearer could live under a rubbish heap for weeks and emerge as if freshly groomed for a ball). Once attuned, the cleansing effect extends beyond clothing to the wearer's own body, and its light adds two dice to Resistance rolls against disease or poison. Crafted from any of the Five Magical Materials, including soulsteel.
compatibility: Any Exalt; explicitly noted as popular among Dragon-Blooded for status display as much as utility.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Sample Artifacts' -> 'Collar of Dawn's Cleansing Light', printed pp. 40-41 (PDF 41-42). Artifact Traits as printed: Power •, Usefulness •, Series Impact •, Script Immunity ••; Drawback • (Component •).

name: Mask (Artifact ••)
summary: Level Two sample artifact: a plain ivory face mask that lets an Exalt alter her appearance to look like anyone she wishes and fully control the emotions her face shows, a fixture of Exalted political and emotional intrigue since the First Age.
requirements: Attunement (5 motes of Essence, the normal cost for a Level •• item).
mechanics: Adds four dice to the wearer's Intelligence + Larceny pool for any disguise attempt (see core Exalted, p. 255). Once attuned, also grants an extra four dice to any attempt to misdirect others about the wearer's true motives, such as relevant Presence, Socialize, or Bureaucracy rolls.
compatibility: Any Exalt; this is the same sample item used as this chapter's Power/Game-Impact worked example (see artifact-creation-rating-framework), where its usefulness against Sidereals specifically is called out as weak ('a child's toy to Sidereals').
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Sample Artifacts' -> 'Mask', printed p. 41 (PDF 42). Artifact Traits as printed: Power ••, Usefulness ••, Series Impact •••, Plot Immunity •• (printed as 'Plot Immunity' here rather than 'Script Immunity', likely an editing inconsistency within the same book); Drawback ••• (Essence •, Component ••).

name: Ring of Being (Artifact ••••)
summary: Level Four sample artifact: one of a small number of rings forged by the legendary Twilight artificer Jervon, each a pure and perfect representation of its Magical Material, that renders its wearer's innate form and mind untouchable by magic, spirits, the Wyld, or demonic influence.
requirements: Attunement (15 motes of Essence); the Exalt can only attune to a ring made of her own kind's appropriate Magical Material (e.g. a Lunar gains no benefit from a jade ring beyond its beauty). No known soulsteel Rings of Being exist -- the secret of making one was lost before the Deathlords rose.
mechanics: While attuned, no magic or power of the dead, the Fair Folk, demons, spirits, or the Wyld can alter the wearer's innate form or mind: she can still be harmed by physical attacks or effects, but no spirit's Charms, no Wyld chaos, no spell can addle her mind or compel her love, and no demon can claim her soul. The exact non-Magical-Material ingredients needed to forge one (at least a sample of the Deep Wyld and possibly a fragment of the Labyrinth) are only partially recorded.
compatibility: Any Exalt, restricted to a ring forged from that Exalt-type's own appropriate Magical Material (a documented orichalcum example was worn by the Solar Deliberative's Hierophant; other Magical-Material versions are rumored to have gone to Lunar, Sidereal, and Terrestrial Exalted).
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Sample Artifacts' -> 'Ring of Being', printed pp. 41-42 (PDF 42-43). Artifact Traits as printed: Power ••••, Usefulness ••••, Series Impact •••, Script Immunity ••••; Drawback •••• (Component ••••).

name: Wings of the Raptor (Artifact ••••)
summary: Level Four sample artifact: a heavy cloak, first built by an earthbound Solar to join his Lunar love in flight, that transforms into a 20-foot wingspan granting true flight along with enhanced aerial combat and sight.
requirements: Attunement (10 motes of Essence to transform from cloak to wings; the spent Essence cannot be reclaimed until the wings revert to their mundane cloak form).
mechanics: While flying: moves at five times the wearer's base running speed (80 mph); adds six dice to Dexterity rolls involving aerial maneuvering, including dodging and hand-to-hand combat; adds six dice to sight-based Perception rolls and reduces distance penalties by three. A flying character can only be attacked in hand-to-hand combat during the initiative tick when she herself attacks in hand-to-hand combat; opponents who want to reach her outside that tick must reflexively close to hand-to-hand range at a -3 penalty (-1 for long weapons like spears), while she may attack or counterattack freely. Ranged attacks against a flying wearer are unaffected by this restriction.
compatibility: Any Exalt.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Sample Artifacts' -> 'Wings of the Raptor', printed pp. 42-43 (PDF 43-44). Artifact Traits as printed: Power ••••, Usefulness •••, Series Impact •••, Script Immunity ••••; Drawback •••• (Component ••••).

name: Soul Mirror (Artifact •••••)
summary: Level Five sample artifact: a soulsteel grand daiklave forged for the Lover Clad in Raiment of Tears' champion, lost after her nemissary fell to two Dragon-Blooded martial artists, that drains Essence and Willpower on every hit and traps the souls of those it kills.
requirements: Attunement (the same Essence cost as an ordinary grand daiklave; see core Exalted, p. 342); all other statistics match a mundane grand daiklave except for an additional (fourth) Hearthstone setting on the handle.
mechanics: On a successful hit, drains one point of the target's temporary Willpower and a number of motes of Essence equal to the wielder's permanent Essence (half, rounded down, passes to the wielder; the rest is consumed by the sword). Anyone the blade kills has their ghost drawn into Soul Mirror instead of the Underworld or Lethe, visible tormented in the flat blade until consumed; the wielder may consume a trapped soul at any time to add 1 to the weapon's speed, accuracy, and damage for seven days (up to four consumed souls' benefits active at once). Any player whose character faces Soul Mirror in battle must succeed at a Willpower roll (difficulty 4 for mortals, 3 for Exalted/other magical beings, 2 for Solars or Abyssals) or suffer a four-die penalty to attack rolls. As a reflexive action costing one contained soul and all of the wielder's remaining peripheral Essence (requires at least 10 Essence in the peripheral pool), the wielder may negate any single attack that would drop her to Incapacitated or below, triggering an anima flare, healing all lethal/bashing damage from that strike, and healing aggravated damage equal to her permanent Essence.
compatibility: Any Exalt capable of wielding a grand daiklave; currently lost, its location unknown.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Sample Artifacts' -> 'Soul Mirror', printed pp. 43-44 (PDF 44-45). Artifact Traits as printed: Power •••••, Usefulness ••••, Series Impact •••••, Script Immunity •••••; Drawback ••••••• (Component ••, Notoriety ••••). This is the final entry of Chapter Two's 'Sample Artifacts' section.

name: Warstriders: History, Appearance, and the Five Design Classes
summary: GM/lore-facing overview of warstriders as a category of First Age/Shogunate/modern siege armor: their history from the Solar Deliberative through the Usurpation and Contagion to the Age of Sorrows, the three broad design eras (First Age, Shogunate, Modern), and the five basic design classes (Scout, Common, Noble, Royal, Juggernaut).
mechanics: Warstriders are giant powered suits of armor, 16 to 30 feet tall, worn rather than piloted like a vehicle. Only three Age-of-Sorrows factions field them extensively: the Realm's legions, Lookshy's Seventh Legion, and the Deathlords' armies; the standard deployment unit is the 'fang' (five warstriders plus supporting infantry/officers, totaling talon size). Sidereals historically made the least use of warstriders of any Exalt type -- starmetal scarcity meant only a handful were ever built, nearly all First Age manufacture, carefully hidden before the Usurpation and rarely deployed since (see artifact-creation-sidereal-notes for related starmetal-scarcity lore). Design classes, by era: First Age warstriders were individualistic and ornamental, experimenting with built-in weapons/devices; Shogunate designs were utilitarian and regimented, with lesser versions of First Age weaponry; Modern warstriders (post-Contagion) are often mismatched assemblages of salvaged parts, usually lacking First Age Essence weapons. The five basic classes (statted in warstrider-scout/-common/-noble/-royal/-juggernaut below) emerged from First Age battlefield experimentation and remain the standard typology used in the Age of Sorrows.
compatibility: Storyteller/setting reference for any Exalt encountering or discussing warstriders; not itself a player-selectable trait. Sidereal-specific deployment/rarity notes are called out because they bear directly on how (rarely) a Sidereal PC would plausibly acquire one.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, unheaded introduction plus 'Appearance' -> 'First Age'/'Shogunate'/'Modern', 'Operation' intro, 'Deployment in the Second Age' -> 'The Realm'/'Lookshy'/'The Deathlords'/'Others', and 'Classes of Warstriders' intro, printed pp. 144-149 (PDF 145-150). The 'Too Many Warstriders!' Storyteller sidebar (printed p. 148/PDF 149, on tuning per-legion deployment density) is summarized here rather than separately inventoried, as a pure Storyteller-tuning note with no player-facing content.

name: Wearing a Warstrider: Operation, Attunement, and Essence Costs
summary: GM-facing mechanical rules for how a character straps into and operates a warstrider: familiarization time, the attunement/Hearthstone-power link, low-power stance, and which kinds of beings (spirits, the dead, the Fair Folk, mortals/God-Blooded) can use one and under what restrictions.
requirements: Ability to channel and commit Essence to artifacts; a warstrider additionally requires a Hearthstone (usually from a level-three Manse) to operate at full power.
mechanics: Familiarization requires no roll but takes (10 - permanent Essence) days to learn to optimize attunement and move well in the control system. Attunement costs 10 motes of Essence in most cases (more for some First Age-weapon-equipped suits) and takes about five minutes to establish or fade, mirroring the time needed to don/remove the armor; while attuned, damage that breaches the armor also harms the wearer via feedback. A warstrider drains its mounted Hearthstone entirely to power itself (the wearer gains no personal benefit from that stone while it's installed); lacking a Hearthstone, a wearer can self-power the suit at 5 motes + 1 Willpower per turn plus 1 mote per action (including movement), though most Second Age warstriders aren't built to sustain this long. Low-power stance (six minus permanent Essence turns to toggle, with proper Hearthstone) cuts maintenance accrual to one-third rate, allows a Hearthstone one level lower, halves movement, halves weapon speed/rate, adds two successes to the already-existing small-target attack penalty, subtracts two dice from attacks/dodges/parries, and reduces initiative by 5. Spirits with a warstrider as part of their panoply can materialize already attuned. The dead pay double Essence commitment to attune to non-soulsteel warstriders and can only use them while materialized or animating a corpse; hungry ghosts generally lack the discipline to operate one. The Fair Folk do not use warstriders by disposition, though an individual fae could choose to. Mortals/God-Blooded with the appropriate Merits (Exalted Players Guide) can attune using normal rules, limited mainly by their scant Essence and lack of penalty-reducing Charms.
compatibility: Any Exalt (or qualifying spirit, ghost, Fair Folk, mortal, or God-Blooded) who can attune to artifacts and gains access to a warstrider and its required Hearthstone.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Operation' -> body text, 'Essence Costs', 'Low-Power Stance', and 'Wearing Warstriders' (including the 'Stealth and Camouflage' sidebar on general adaptive-camouflage/mundane-camouflage rules, printed pp. 152-153/PDF 153-154, which is a general Stealth-rules digression rather than warstrider-specific and is summarized rather than separately inventoried), printed pp. 146, 150-153 (PDF 147, 151-154).
cost: 10 motes (attunement, typical); 5 motes + 1 Willpower/turn + 1 mote/action if self-powering without a Hearthstone

name: Warstrider Benefits and Limitations (Strength, Armor, Size, Vision, Manipulation, Stealth)
summary: GM-facing summary of the mechanical upsides (superhuman Strength, restful endurance, heavy hardened armor, high durability against being permanently destroyed) and downsides (size-driven collateral damage, a three-success penalty attacking human-scaled targets, +2 difficulty on fine-manipulation tasks, a four-die Awareness/Perception penalty from limited vision and hearing, fatigue/mobility penalties, and near-total lack of a Stealth pool while moving) of wearing a warstrider.
mechanics: Benefits: warstrider Strength (typically 10+, see the class table in warstrider-scout etc.) replaces the wearer's Strength only for damage, lifting/carrying, breaking objects, and jumping distance (not other purposes); Charms that enhance the wearer's Strength apply to the warstrider too; locked limbs let the wearer rest without fatigue; heavy armor grants both soak and Hardness (ignoring attacks that don't exceed half its soak); warstriders are never treated as inanimate objects for damage purposes (all damage dice are rolled normally) and are resistant to being permanently destroyed. Limitations: brushing an obstacle inflicts damage as if exerting half the warstrider's Strength on the Feats of Strength table, falling/smashing into something inflicts full Strength, and being forcefully hurled into something doubles it; attacking any target under 10 feet tall subtracts three successes from the attack roll; movement rate is multiplied by 10 (modified further by design); fine-manipulation tasks suffer +2 difficulty and human-scaled weapons impose a two-success penalty (if usable at all); vision is reduced to a forward slit view (no peripheral vision) and hearing is muffled, imposing a four-die penalty on Awareness/Perception rolls; control-frame fatigue drives frequent fatigue checks and mobility penalties on agility-based pools; a warstrider has no natural Stealth pool while moving (ambush from cover/camouflage is still possible), and tracking one is trivial (untracseable disguise Charms increase relevant difficulties by 3, or force a Wits + Survival roll at difficulty 3 if none would normally be needed).
compatibility: Any Exalt wearing a warstrider; Charms that reduce/eliminate fatigue, mobility, or perception penalties (common among habitual warstrider wearers) work normally against these limitations.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Warstrider Benefits' -> 'Strength'/'Endurance'/'Heavy Armor'/'Nonhumanoid Warstriders'/'Durability' and 'Warstrider Limitations' -> 'Size'/'Massive Weapons'/'Mobility'/'Charms'/'Limits of Strength'/'Limited Manipulation'/'Limited Vision'/'Fatigue and Mobility'/'Stealth', printed pp. 149-152 (PDF 150-153). The 'Nonhumanoid Warstriders' subsection (on rare Lunar-shifter-compatible and automaton designs) is folded into this summary rather than separately inventoried, as pure setting flavor with no distinct mechanic.

name: Warstrider Maintenance and Repair
summary: GM-facing rules for the upkeep a warstrider needs to stay functional: technician requirements, tool/material costs, the escalating penalties for falling behind on maintenance, and how to repair accrued damage.
requirements: Warstriders carry the Maintenance ••• Drawback (see artifact-drawback-and-power-sources) and require a technician with Lore •••••, Occult ••••, and Craft (First Age Weapons) •••• to service.
mechanics: Requires one hour of maintenance per 10 hours of operation (heavy labor/combat hours count double); tools cost Resources •••• (fills a workshop or two two-horse carts, taking six hours to set up a mobile workspace); every 40 hours of maintenance (or each repair roll) consumes Resources ••• worth of jade, reagents, and parts. For every 10 hours in arrears (accruing only once un-attuned), the warstrider suffers one escalating penalty (GM's choice or in order): -2L/2B soak (and Hardness, if used); -1 to ground speed multiplier (or speed/maneuver if flying); +2 difficulty to hit sub-10-foot targets; loss of one special power/ability; or a one-die penalty to all physical actions while worn. Removing a penalty requires performing twice the arrears-amount of maintenance; Storytellers may rule severe arrears (3+ penalties) permanent, requiring a difficulty-3 Intelligence + Craft (First Age Weapons) repair roll per hour per penalty (difficulty 5 and extra time/manpower for complex repairs like a severed limb); repairs cannot be performed while maintenance is still in arrears.
compatibility: Storyteller/technician-player tool for any warstrider owner, including a Sidereal who somehow acquires one; not a player trait in itself.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Maintenance', printed pp. 151-152 (PDF 152-153).

name: Scout Warstrider (Artifact •••)
summary: Lightest and fastest of the five basic warstrider design classes: a 16-foot suit built for mobility and reconnaissance over raw armor and damage, often enchanted to reduce its detectability, though rarer than common warstriders since few valued its tradeoffs.
requirements: Attunement per the standard warstrider rules (see warstrider-operation-and-essence-costs); requires a Hearthstone (or self-powering) to run at full capability.
mechanics: Soak 16L/16B (Hardness 8, i.e. half soak); Strength 10; Mobility Penalty -3; Fatigue Value 4; base Artifact rating ••• for the bare suit before weapons/enchantments are added.
compatibility: Any Exalt who can attune to a warstrider and obtains one; historically built in smaller numbers than common warstriders and rarely fielded by Sidereals given starmetal scarcity (see warstrider-overview-and-classes).
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Classes of Warstriders' -> 'Scout' (printed p. 148/PDF 149) and the 'Basic Warstrider Designs' table (printed p. 154/PDF 155), row 'Scout'.

name: Common Warstrider (Artifact •••)
summary: The backbone infantry-class warstrider design, standing about six yards (18 feet) tall: the most numerous warstrider type in the Age of Sorrows, typically jade-forged for Terrestrial Exalted use and forming the majority of the Realm's and Lookshy's warstrider forces.
requirements: Attunement per the standard warstrider rules (see warstrider-operation-and-essence-costs); requires a Hearthstone (or self-powering) to run at full capability.
mechanics: Soak 20L/20B (Hardness 10); Strength 12; Mobility Penalty -6; Fatigue Value 6; base Artifact rating ••• for the bare suit before weapons/enchantments are added.
compatibility: Any Exalt who can attune to a warstrider and obtains one; the most commonly available class, though still a major undertaking to acquire outside a major military power.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Classes of Warstriders' -> 'Common' (printed p. 149/PDF 150) and the 'Basic Warstrider Designs' table (printed p. 154/PDF 155), row 'Common'. This is also the class marking 'the limit of Creation's ability to build new warstriders' -- neither the Realm nor Lookshy have built classes beyond Common since shortly after the Shogunate's fall.

name: Noble Warstrider (Artifact ••••)
summary: A 20-foot-tall warstrider class favored by the Celestial Exalted, stronger, more responsive, and more heavily armored than common suits; the Celestial Exalted are the only Exalted type to retain the secrets of building noble warstriders in the Age of Sorrows, though even Lunars and Sidereals rarely do so.
requirements: Attunement per the standard warstrider rules (see warstrider-operation-and-essence-costs); requires a Hearthstone (or self-powering) to run at full capability.
mechanics: Soak 22L/22B; Strength 14; Mobility Penalty -4; Fatigue Value 4; base Artifact rating •••• for the bare suit before weapons/enchantments are added. The Scarlet Empress's personal warstrider, Unyielding Fury of Righteousness, is called out as a rare Second-Age-built example of this class.
compatibility: Celestial Exalted (Solar, Lunar, Sidereal, Abyssal) who can attune to a warstrider and obtain one; Sidereal ownership is exceptionally rare given starmetal scarcity and this splat's minimal warstrider tradition (see warstrider-overview-and-classes).
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Classes of Warstriders' -> 'Noble' (printed p. 149/PDF 150) and the 'Basic Warstrider Designs' table (printed p. 154/PDF 155), row 'Noble'.

name: Royal Warstrider (Artifact •••••)
summary: A rare, legendary 25-foot warstrider class wielded almost exclusively by Solars and a scant handful of Lunars in the First Age; only a tiny number survive in the Age of Sorrows, and most orichalcum examples are too heavy for Terrestrials to attune, while any built since the Contagion are grim soulsteel-and-Abyssal-iron war machines serving the Deathlords.
requirements: Attunement per the standard warstrider rules (see warstrider-operation-and-essence-costs), though many surviving orichalcum examples require more committable Essence than most Terrestrial Exalted possess; requires a Hearthstone (or self-powering) to run at full capability.
mechanics: Soak 24L/24B; Strength 16; Mobility Penalty -2; Fatigue Value 2; base Artifact rating ••••• for the bare suit before weapons/enchantments are added.
compatibility: Historically Solar and (rarely) Lunar Exalted; post-Contagion examples are built of soulsteel/Abyssal iron for Deathlord-aligned Abyssals. Effectively unobtainable for a Sidereal PC barring extraordinary circumstances -- included for completeness of the design-class table.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Classes of Warstriders' -> 'Royal' (printed p. 149/PDF 150) and the 'Basic Warstrider Designs' table (printed p. 154/PDF 155), row 'Royal'.

name: Juggernaut Warstrider (Artifact •••••)
summary: A ponderously slow but nearly indestructible 20-foot-tall siege/combat-engineering warstrider class, nearly twice as wide as a common warstrider and second in armor only to skyships and a few ocean-going craft; few survived the Contagion, and some Abyssal deathknights favor the class for raw destructive power.
requirements: Attunement per the standard warstrider rules (see warstrider-operation-and-essence-costs); requires a Hearthstone (or self-powering) to run at full capability.
mechanics: Soak 30L/30B; Strength 20; Mobility Penalty -10; Fatigue Value 8; base Artifact rating ••••• for the bare suit before weapons/enchantments are added.
compatibility: Any Exalt who can attune to a warstrider and obtains one; only scant handfuls remain in the armories of the Realm and Lookshy, and some are used by Abyssal deathknights.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Classes of Warstriders' -> 'Juggernaut' (printed p. 149/PDF 150) and the 'Basic Warstrider Designs' table (printed p. 154/PDF 155), row 'Juggernaut'.

name: Warstrider Weaponry: Mounting Rules and Weapon-Location Requirements
summary: GM-facing rules for how built-in weapons are mounted on a warstrider (arm/shoulder/torso locations, shared-Essence attunement discount, independent maintenance) and a reference summary of the weapon-location-requirements table cataloging which weapon types go where.
mechanics: Most built-in weapons occupy a single mounting location (arm, shoulder-pivot, or chest); larger weapons (e.g. an implosion bow) need multiple locations (arms plus a backpack). Built-in artifact weapons draw spare Essence from an installed Hearthstone, halving that weapon's normal attunement mote cost and adding the (halved) result to the warstrider's own commitment; weapons needing a mounted Hearthstone or other material component (bound elementals, etc.) still need it, assumed placed conveniently for the pilot. Weapon maintenance is tracked separately from the warstrider's own maintenance and cannot be performed simultaneously. Weapon-location summary: brawling aids and hand-to-hand weapons (swords/axes/maces/flails) are always arm-mounted (cannot mount in limbs lacking hands); large hand-to-hand weapons (lances/spears/pole axes/great swords) are usually not mounted (carried instead); longbows/shortbows mount in one arm but need both to fire; projectile launchers (bolt launcher, dart thrower, fire projector, chain dagger) mount per their own entries; the warstrider fire lance and shock ram are frequently shoulder/torso mounted or must be arm mounted respectively; the warstrider implosion bow is normally carried two-handed with a backpack, or if mounted takes a full arm plus a backpack/torso location; medium Essence cannons can share an arm with a brawling aid or another small cannon.
compatibility: Storyteller/artificer-player tool for any warstrider owner outfitting built-in weapons; not a player trait in itself.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Warstrider Weaponry' -> 'Built-In Artifact Weapons' and the 'Weapon Location Requirements' table, printed pp. 154-155 (PDF 155-156).

name: Warstrider-Scaled Mundane Weapons (Hand-to-Hand and Ranged)
summary: Reference stat tables for the mundane (non-artifact), warstrider-scaled melee weapons (Axe, Chopping Sword, Fighting Gauntlet, Hook Sword, Mace, Punch Blade, Spear, Staff, Sword, Two-Handed Sword, plus unarmed Punch/Kick) and ranged weapons (Shortbow, Longbow, Bolt Launcher, Dart Thrower, Fire Projector) sized for a warstrider wearer, along with warstrider ammunition costs and arrow-type notes.
mechanics: Melee weapons (Speed/Accuracy/Damage/Defense/min. Strength/Dexterity as printed): Punch (spd 3, +3L, no min stats), Kick (spd -6, +5L, Dex 2), Axe (spd -3, acc -1, +10L, def -2, Str 12, cost ••••), Chopping Sword (spd -3, acc +1, +10L, def -1, Str 12, cost ••••), Fighting Gauntlet (spd +3, +5L, Str 10, cost •••), Hook Sword (spd -3, acc -1, +7L, def +3, Str 12, Dex/MA 4, cost •••••), Mace (spd 0, acc +1, +7L, Str 12, cost ••••, piercing), Punch Blade (spd +1, acc +1, +6L, Str 10, cost •••, piercing, armor-mount-designed), Spear (spd 0, +7L, def +1, Str 10, cost •••), Staff (spd +2, acc +1, +7L, def +2, Str 10, cost ••), Sword (spd -3, acc +1, +8L, def +1, Str 12, cost ••••), Two-Handed Sword (spd -6, +14L, def -1, Str 14, cost •••••). Ranged weapons require ammunition costing Resources •• per turn's worth of fire (one arrow, four bolts, or six dart clusters); half of all fired arrows are lost. Shortbow/Longbow (acc +1, damage by arrow type, rate 1, cost ••••, min Str 12/14, range 250/350); Bolt Launcher (acc +0, 10L piercing, rate 1/4 with a four-round magazine requiring four turns to rewind, cost •••, range 150); Dart Thrower (acc +4, 5L piercing, rate 1/2, cost •••, range 100); Fire Projector (acc +1, 12L, rate 1 with a five-barrel double-load of firedust, cost ••••, range 20, no extended range). name: Proteus Gauntlet (Artifact ••••)
summary: A First Age moonsilver smashfist scaled for warstrider use that can reshape itself into any standard warstrider-scale weapon on demand, solving the problem that warstriders can rarely carry more than one or two built-in weapons at a time.
requirements: Attunement (6 motes of Essence); non-Lunars pay double the normal Essence cost to gain the weapon's Magical Material (moonsilver) bonus.
mechanics: As a non-rolled action, the attuned wearer can shift the gauntlet into the form of any standard warstrider-scale weapon for 1 mote per shift. If shifted into a weapon needing ammunition, it comes preloaded with one turn's worth (or one magazine, for weapons with one); once that ammunition is expended, no more can be created until the existing ammunition is physically retrieved.
compatibility: Any warstrider wearer who can attune to it, though non-Lunars pay a Magical-Material-bonus surcharge; a Sidereal wielder is plausible but rare given the class's overall scarcity of warstriders.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Proteus Gauntlet (Artifact ••••)', printed p. 159 (PDF 160), immediately following the Artifact Ranged Weapons table and prose weapon descriptions.

name: The Limits of Sorcery
summary: GM/player-facing system-wide statement of the four hard limits on sorcery's power, regardless of circle: time cannot be altered, celestial bodies are outside sorcery's reach, death cannot be reversed, and geomancy cannot be directly conjured.
mechanics: Time is immutable: no time travel is possible via sorcery, and sorcerous divination is only modestly better than mortal astrology in reliability/speed. Celestial events (sun, moon, planets, stars, comets) lie outside sorcery's purview -- only at the discretion of the Maidens and other Celestial officials, effectively impossible in practice. Death is irrevocable: ghosts can be summoned/bound and the Underworld can be visited, but there is no sorcerous resurrection; necromancy is a weaker art for sorcerers than for true necromancers, and summoning ghosts or creating zombies requires at least Celestial Circle (easier at Solar Circle). Geomancy cannot be altered directly: sorcery cannot conjure a Demesne outright, though costly Celestial Circle spells can raise a Manse or enable landscaping that indirectly reshapes geomancy, provided the caster understands Manse architecture and geomantic principle.
compatibility: Any sorcerer of any circle, including Sidereal sorcerers; a foundational constraint on what any spell (see the Terrestrial/Celestial Circle spell catalog already inventoried) can accomplish.
notes: Chapter One: Magical Theory, 'The Limits of Sorcery' sidebar, printed pp. 11-12 (PDF 12-13).

name: The Black and White Treatises (Sorcery Primer Texts)
summary: The two most common written texts on sorcery in the Age of Sorrows: The White Treatise, a self-initiation-capable primer on Terrestrial Circle theory and the five-station model, and The Black Treatise, a companion volume containing the five oldest and most common Terrestrial spells (Death of Obsidian Butterflies, Demon of the First Circle, Emerald Countermagic, Invulnerable Skin of Bronze, and Stormwind Rider).
requirements: Wits + Bureaucracy roll (difficulty 4) to locate both volumes in the Threshold, waived if the character is in the good graces of a sorcerous academy (e.g. the Heptagram or the Academy of Sorcery).
mechanics: Cost Resources •••• each (Resources •• each if the good-graces waiver applies). The White Treatise alone is sufficient to self-initiate into the Terrestrial Circle, though only to a minimal degree of technique and theory. Students at the Heptagram and the Academy of Sorcery are issued at least The White Treatise early in their education, making it comparatively easy to obtain within the civilized world.
compatibility: Any character seeking to self-initiate into or study Terrestrial Circle sorcery, including a Sidereal Exalt (who more commonly learns via institutional tutelage instead, per sorcery-sidereal-initiation-notes).
notes: Chapter One: Magical Theory, 'The Black and White Treatises', printed pp. 10-11 (PDF 11-12); the five spells named as The Black Treatise's contents are core-rulebook Terrestrial Circle spells, not separately re-inventoried here.
cost: Resources •••• each (or •• each in a sorcerous academy's good graces)

name: The Five Unavoidable Challenges (Five-Station Initiation Model)
summary: GM/character-creation-facing narrative framework describing the five universal trials (Humility, Tutelage, Journey, Fear, and Choice/Sacrifice, mapped to the Dawn/Zenith/Twilight/Night/Eclipse castes) that every Terrestrial Circle sorcery initiate must pass, regardless of school or mentor.
mechanics: Dawn station (Humility): enduring hardship, labor, or thankless service without resisting pressure. Zenith station (Tutelage): learning to recognize and accept wisdom from an unlikely mentor (often a non-sorcerer, spirit, or mortal). Twilight station (Journey): learning that a seemingly pointless physical journey through wild, untamed places has its own immanent value. Night station (Fear): confronting and mastering one of the initiate's own darkest fears. Eclipse station (Choice): making a genuine, costly sacrifice (a valued relationship, ideal, or possession) to cross the final threshold; sacrifice value scales with the circle sought (a finger or vice for Terrestrial; love or friendship for Celestial and above). No mechanical die-roll system governs pass/fail -- these are Storyteller-adjudicated narrative beats, and initiation should take at least as long as the training time normally required to learn sorcery.
compatibility: Any Exalt undergoing sorcerous initiation into any circle, including a Sidereal pursuing Celestial (Sapphire) Circle initiation; purely a narrative/character-creation framework with no additional mechanical restriction on who can learn sorcery.
notes: Chapter One: Magical Theory, 'The Five Stations', 'The Five Unavoidable Challenges' sidebar, and 'The Perils of Initiation' sidebar, printed pp. 12-15 (PDF 13-16). The parallel 'Celestial and Solar Circles' initiation-sacrifice discussion (printed pp. 14-15/PDF 15-16) and the Great Curse's interaction with sorcerous hubris are folded into this summary rather than separately inventoried, as narrative color rather than distinct mechanics.

name: Sidereal Sorcery Initiation: Efficient, Institutional, and Early
summary: Sidereal-specific lore on how the Chosen of the Maidens are trained in sorcery: quickly, institutionally (Silurian teaching technique plus Salinan notation, mirroring the Heptagram's methods), and almost universally to at least the Terrestrial Circle, typically reaching the Celestial Circle before the sorcerer's first century of existence.
mechanics: Sidereal sorcery tutelage functions like a 'sorcerer mill': technical mastery is prioritized over personal growth or spiritual self-mastery, in contrast to (for example) the No Moons' vision-quest-inflected teaching. Almost every member of the Five-Score Fellowship undergoes at least Terrestrial Circle initiation, since Sidereals view the sacrifice required (see sorcery-five-stations-initiation) as comparatively minor next to the sacrifices already demanded by service to Fate. Most Sidereals master the Celestial Circle very early in their lives, usually within their first century.
compatibility: Sidereal Exalted specifically; useful color for framing why a given Sidereal PC sorcerer-character reached the Celestial Circle so quickly (or, unusually, has not).
notes: Chapter One: Magical Theory, 'Sidereals' sidebar (within the broader 'Schools of Thought'/per-Exalt-type initiation survey alongside 'No Moons'), printed pp. 15-16 (PDF 16-17).

name: Summoning Demons and Elementals: Principles, Binding, and Risk
summary: GM-facing procedural summary of how a sorcerer summons and binds an individual demon or elemental: general summoning principles, the psychological cracks that make a demon's mind bindable, binding-oath mechanics, choosing a target, running the summoning ritual (including a budget 'summoning on the cheap' option), surviving the process, and what happens if the summoner dies while a spirit remains sworn to her.
requirements: Access to a summoning spell of the appropriate circle (see the Terrestrial/Celestial Circle spell catalog already inventoried); summoning a bound spirit is a roleplay- and negotiation-heavy process layered on top of the spell's own casting requirements.
mechanics: Demons: 'Cracks in the Demon Mind' catalogs the psychological vulnerabilities (pride, obsession, unfinished business, etc.) a summoner can exploit to compel service; 'Binding Oaths' covers the wording and enforcement of the geas that binds a summoned demon; 'Choosing a Demon' and 'The Summoning' walk through target selection and ritual execution, with 'Summoning on the Cheap' offering a reduced-cost/reduced-reliability variant; 'Surviving the Summoning' covers the dangers of a botched or resisted binding, and 'Death While Sworn' resolves what happens to a bound demon's obligations if its summoner dies. Elementals: 'Elemental Snares' and 'Choosing an Elemental' parallel the demon-selection process for elemental spirits, 'The Summoning' covers ritual execution, and 'Summoning the Already Bound' covers negotiating for or seizing an elemental already bound into someone else's service (e.g. a Manse's resident elemental).
compatibility: Any sorcerer PC (including a Sidereal) casting a demon- or elemental-summoning spell; this is Storyteller-facing procedural and roleplay guidance layered on top of the spells themselves, not a separate player trait.
notes: Chapter Four: Practical Summonings, 'Demons' -> 'Principles'/'Cracks in the Demon Mind'/'Binding Oaths'/'Choosing a Demon'/'The Summoning'/'Summoning on the Cheap'/'Surviving the Summoning'/'Death While Sworn' and 'Elementals' -> 'Elemental Snares'/'Choosing an Elemental'/'The Summoning'/'Other Approaches'/'Summoning the Already Bound', printed pp. 71-79 (PDF 72-80).

name: Summoning's Social and Political Context (Immaculate Philosophy, Realm Law, Elementalist Licenses)
summary: GM/setting reference on the social, religious, and legal framework surrounding elemental (and, to a lesser extent, demonic) summoning in the Age of Sorrows: the Immaculate Philosophy's stance on binding elementals, the Celestial Hierarchy's bureaucratic view of the practice, Realm and Principality of the Shore law, the Wood Dragon Pact governing elemental-summoning rights in the East, and the licensing regime that regulates who may legally summon and hold elementals bound.
mechanics: 'Social Issues' and 'The Immaculate Philosophy' summarize why binding gods and elementals is religiously and socially fraught within Immaculate-aligned territory. 'The Celestial Hierarchy' and 'The Realm' cover how Yu-Shan's bureaucracy and the Scarlet Empire's law treat elemental summoning and ownership. 'The Principality of the Shore' and 'Elementals of the Shore' detail that region's distinct elemental-summoning customs. 'The Wood Dragon Pact' and 'The Three Wood Dragons' describe an Eastern treaty regime governing which elementals may be bound and by whom. 'Licensing and Permissions' and 'Elementalist Licenses' cover the formal Realm-issued licenses required to legally summon, hold, or trade in bound elementals, and 'Outside of the Realm' notes how enforcement (and its absence) varies beyond Realm-controlled territory.
compatibility: Storyteller/setting reference for any sorcerer summoning or trading in bound elementals, including a Sidereal sorcerer operating within or against Realm/Immaculate jurisdiction; not itself a player trait.
notes: Chapter Four: Practical Summonings, 'Social Issues' through 'Elementalist Licenses'/'Outside of the Realm', printed pp. 77-82 (PDF 78-83).

name: Mass Summoning Projects (Planning, Scope, and Time Requirements)
summary: GM-facing rules for large-scale summoning projects that bind many spirits at once (e.g. staffing a factory-cathedral or elemental-powered fleet) rather than a single individual: project planning and scoping, the mass summoning ritual itself, Yozi-possession risk at extreme scale, and the time required across a project's early stages, task execution, task conclusion, and denouement.
requirements: Typically requires Celestial Circle sorcery or greater and substantial Resources/labor investment; intended for chronicle-level or Storyteller-directed projects rather than routine individual spellcasting.
mechanics: 'Planning' and 'Project Scope' cover how a sorcerer (or, more often, an institution) defines the scale and purpose of a mass summoning before beginning. 'Summoning' and 'Mass Summoning Rules' cover the ritual mechanics of binding many spirits simultaneously, while 'Yozi Possession' flags the escalated risk of drawing the attention or influence of a Yozi when summoning at very large scale. 'Time Requirements for Mass Summoning' breaks the project into 'Early Stages,' 'Task Execution,' 'Task Conclusion,' and 'Denouement' phases, each with its own time investment and complication profile.
compatibility: Storyteller/institution-level tool for chronicle-scale summoning projects; a Sidereal sorcerer might direct or oversee such a project as a plot within a larger Bronze/Gold Faction initiative, but this is not an individual player trait.
notes: Chapter Four: Practical Summonings, 'Planning' through 'Time Requirements for Mass Summoning' -> 'Early Stages'/'Task Execution'/'Task Conclusion'/'Denouement', printed pp. 83-86 (PDF 84-87).

name: Bound Spirit Limit Profiles (Courtesan, Ecstatic, Functionary, Horror, Hunter, Killer, Slave, Vizier, Warden, Sufferer, and Minor Profiles)
summary: GM-facing psychological-archetype toolkit for running a bound demon or elemental as an ongoing NPC servant: 10 major personality Limit Profiles (plus minor profiles) each defining a Weakness, Limit Conditions that build toward rebellion, a Limit Break (what the spirit does when it snaps), ways of Reducing Limit, and Practical Management advice, each with separate demon and elemental variants.
mechanics: Each profile (The Courtesan, The Ecstatic, The Functionary, The Horror, The Hunter, The Killer, The Slave, The Vizier, The Warden, and the Minor Profiles including The Sufferer) follows the same five-part structure: Weakness (the psychological vulnerability that defines the archetype), Limit Conditions (triggers that accumulate Limit), Limit Break (the archetype-specific crisis/rebellion that occurs at maximum Limit, ranging from passive-aggressive sabotage to open violence), Reducing Limit (how a summoner can manage or de-escalate the spirit's building resentment), and Practical Management (Storyteller advice for running the bound spirit day-to-day), each further split into Demon and Elemental variant notes.
compatibility: Storyteller tool for running any bound demon or elemental as a recurring NPC servant/asset for a sorcerer PC (including a Sidereal); not a player-facing trait, and not broken into 10+ individual rows given its purely GM-procedural, non-selectable nature.
notes: Chapter Four: Practical Summonings, 'Limit Profiles' -> 'Limit Rules'/'Limit Conditions'/'Limit Break'/'Reducing Limit' framework intro, followed by 'The Courtesan' through 'The Warden' and the 'Minor Profiles' (including 'The Sufferer'), printed pp. 86-99 (PDF 87-100), running to the end of the chapter just before Chapter Five's spell catalog begins.
